A cassock is a long, plain garment worn by members of the Christian clergy — priests, ministers, deacons, and others who hold religious office in the church.

Picture a coat that starts at the neck and goes all the way down to the ankles or feet. It fits close to the body, has long sleeves, and typically fastens down the front with a row of buttons. It is not loose and flowing like a robe — it is more structured and fitted, almost like a very long, plain overcoat. It has no decorative patterns or elaborate design. Its defining feature is its length: it covers almost the entire body.

The cassock is worn by Christian clergy across many denominations — Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican, and others. It is not exclusive to one type of Christianity; it is a broadly shared tradition across the Christian world.

Beyond priests, it is also worn by:

  • Seminarians (students training to become priests)
  • Altar servers and choir members during religious services
  • Monks and nuns in certain orders

The color of a cassock is not random — it signals the wearer's rank within the church hierarchy:

  • Black — the most common color; worn by ordinary priests and deacons
  • Purple or violet — worn by bishops
  • Red (scarlet) — worn by cardinals
  • White — worn exclusively by the Pope

So if you see someone in a red cassock, you immediately know that person holds the rank of cardinal without needing to be told. The garment itself communicates status.

A cassock can be worn in two distinct contexts:

  1. During religious services and ceremonies — It is part of the official dress of the clergy when performing duties at church: celebrating Mass, conducting baptisms, leading prayers, and so on. In this context, other garments (like a white surplice or a decorated vestment called a chasuble) are often worn on top of the cassock. The cassock, in other words, is the base layer of a priest's ceremonial outfit.
  2. As everyday dress — In more traditional or conservative religious settings, clergy may wear the cassock as their regular daily clothing, not just during services. It marks them as members of the clergy at all times.

The cassock is more than just a piece of clothing. It is a symbol of religious identity and dedication. When a person puts on a cassock, they are visually setting themselves apart from ordinary society, signaling that they have committed their life to religious service. It is a public declaration of their role and calling.

In this sense, seeing a cassock tells you two things at once: the person wearing it belongs to the Christian clergy, and — through its color — where exactly they stand in the religious hierarchy.
A quick way to picture it

Imagine a tall priest standing at the altar of a church, dressed head to toe in black, with a garment that starts at his collar and sweeps all the way down to the floor. That long black garment is the cassock. Now imagine the Pope in the same style of garment, but in pure white. The shape and cut are the same — only the color changes with rank.

A cassock is a long-sleeved, ankle-length, close-fitting garment worn by Christian clergy. It is plain and formal in appearance, covers almost the entire body, and comes in different colors that indicate the wearer's rank in the church (black for priests, purple for bishops, red for cardinals, white for the Pope). It is worn both during religious services — typically as a base layer under other vestments — and sometimes as daily dress, and it serves as a powerful symbol of religious vocation and identity.
